notes: The early-pathways curriculum for the Trades Network: the working world brought into the subjects a school already teaches, from K–2 up. Five tracks — discovering the trades early, the math on the jobsite, the science in the craft, reading and writing the working word, and civics through the working city — so a district can teach fractions on a cut list, energy on a live-wire hazard map (never a live wire), and civic history through its own port and union halls. Transfer checks stay on real material a classroom can hold: rulers, recipes, water, paper specs, public records and observation from safe, public ground. The honesty stances carry verbatim: no union local numbers (the regional council is the front door) and no classroom activity ever counts as equipment certification or union credit.

themes.description: Every classroom is a finished jobsite — walls, wires, pipes, air, light — and each part was somebody's trade.
themes.transfer_check: Point out five things in your own classroom and name the trade that made each one work.

themes.description: Reading a worker by what they carry — the gauge, the trowel, the sling, the meter — and what each tool says the job needs.
themes.transfer_check: Match ten real or pictured tools to their trades and explain one match to somebody using what the tool measures or moves.

themes.description: What a working day actually holds for one trade — the start time, the crew, the tasks, the calls, the cleanup.
themes.transfer_check: Interview a working tradesperson (family, neighbor, or class visitor) and retell their day in order to somebody who wasn't there.

themes.description: Real work is done by crews — the lead, the safety eye, the new hand — and every trade has a way of teaching its next person.
themes.transfer_check: Do one real classroom job as a crew of three with named roles, then swap roles and do it again.

themes.description: What a union is in plain words — workers who band together, the hall where the trade gathers, the apprenticeship that pays you to learn.
themes.transfer_check: Explain to somebody, in your own words, what a union hall is and what an apprentice does there.

themes.description: The network's trade families as a map of the working world — from the crane to the kitchen to the classroom itself.
themes.transfer_check: Sort fifteen trade families into groups you invent, and defend your grouping to somebody who grouped them differently.

themes.description: Every region has its working ground — a port, a pump station, a rail yard — that a learner can see from public, safe ground.
themes.transfer_check: Find, on a real map of your region, three working sites from the network's city maps and name what moves or runs at each.

themes.description: Measuring, sorting, steady hands, clear directions — schoolwork skills that are already trade skills with different names.
themes.transfer_check: Name three things you can already do, match each to a trade that uses it, and demonstrate one of them.

themes.description: Why every trade teaches safety before tools — the flagged line, the rated tag, the call made out loud.
themes.transfer_check: Walk one room or yard and point out three things a tradesperson would check before starting work there.

themes.description: The honest tryout — a cardboard sim, a bench task, a hall visit — and how it differs from the real, certified thing.
themes.transfer_check: Complete one tabletop trade simulation and tell somebody one thing it taught you and one thing it cannot teach you.

themes.description: Length, width, depth with real rulers and tapes — the jobsite's first mathematics, where an error costs material.
themes.transfer_check: Measure a real object three ways, record the numbers, and have a partner check one measurement against yours.

themes.description: Halves, quarters, eighths and sixteenths as carpenters actually use them — the tape measure as a fraction number line.
themes.transfer_check: Mark a strip of paper or wood at three fractional lengths from a cut list and prove one mark by folding or re-measuring.

themes.description: Mortar, concrete, dough and paint all obey ratios — scaling a recipe up and down without breaking it.
themes.transfer_check: Scale a real mix or recipe from four servings to ten, write both versions, and explain what stayed the same.

themes.description: How much paint, how much concrete, how much pipe — turning a room's numbers into a materials order.
themes.transfer_check: Compute the floor area and wall area of a real room and write the materials line for covering one of them.

themes.theme: The right angle and the diagonal
themes.description: The 3-4-5 triangle the trades have used for millennia — squaring a corner with arithmetic instead of guesswork.
themes.transfer_check: Square a real corner or rectangle using the 3-4-5 rule and show the check that proves it square.

themes.description: Roofs shed, ramps climb, drains fall — rise over run as the trades' working fraction.
themes.transfer_check: Measure the slope of a real ramp, roofline (from the ground) or drain and express it as rise over run.

themes.theme: Load, span and the safe number
themes.description: Why the chart on the crane and the table in the code book are mathematics with lives attached — reading limits, never exceeding them.
themes.transfer_check: Read one real rated capacity (a ladder, a strap, an elevator plate) and compute how many of a real load stay under it.

themes.description: Materials plus labor plus the margin — how a tradesperson turns arithmetic into a price the customer can trust.
themes.transfer_check: Write a one-page estimate for a small real task — materials, time, total — and defend one number in it.

themes.theme: The meter is a number over time
themes.description: Kilowatt-hours, gallons per minute, board feet per shift — rates as the mathematics of running work.
themes.transfer_check: Read a real meter (electric, water or gas) twice, a day apart, and compute the rate of use between readings.

themes.description: Close enough, said precisely — plus-or-minus as the machinist's honest promise, and why some work allows a sixteenth and some a thousandth.
themes.transfer_check: Measure five copies of the same object, state the spread, and propose a tolerance the maker could promise.

themes.description: Gravity, pressure and the siphon — the plumber's physics, from the P-trap under every sink to the pump station under the city.
themes.transfer_check: Demonstrate a working siphon or trap with tubing and water and explain why the water moves — or stays.

themes.description: Current, voltage and resistance in the electrician's terms — why the loop must close and why the breaker opens it.
themes.transfer_check: Build a battery-bulb-switch circuit, break it in two different places, and explain why the bulb dies both times.

themes.description: Conduction, convection, radiation — the insulator's science, from the wall's R-value to the coffee cup's sleeve.
themes.transfer_check: Wrap two identical containers of warm water differently, measure both after twenty minutes, and name the heat path you slowed.

themes.theme: The lever, the pulley and the crane
themes.description: Mechanical advantage — how the rigger's block and the operator's boom multiply force, and what they pay for it in distance.
themes.transfer_check: Lift a real load with and without a simple pulley or lever and describe what got easier and what got longer.

themes.description: Wood moves, steel expands, concrete cures — the material science every trade respects, and the joints that forgive it.
themes.transfer_check: Find one real expansion joint, gap or cure date in your neighborhood and explain what it forgives.

themes.description: Concrete hardening, paint drying, bread rising — chemical change on the jobsite, and why time is an ingredient.
themes.transfer_check: Run one safe cure or set (plaster, glue, dough) at two temperatures and report which finished first and why that fits.

themes.description: The suspended load as physics — period, momentum, and why the crane operator's smooth hand is applied science.
themes.transfer_check: Swing a weight on a string at two lengths, time ten swings of each, and state what changed the period.

themes.description: Why the signaller's hands beat shouting, how fiber carries light, and what the working world knows about noise.
themes.transfer_check: Send a short message across a noisy room two ways — voice and agreed hand signals — and report which survived.

themes.description: Wind on the glass lift, rain on the pour, heat on the crew — reading a forecast the way a foreman does.
themes.transfer_check: Take a real three-day forecast and mark which day you would pour, lift or paint outdoors, with the reason.

themes.theme: The experiment is a test fit
themes.description: Hypothesis, trial, measurement, revision — the scientific method as every tradesperson's dry fit before the glue.
themes.transfer_check: Design and run one fair test of a small working question (which tape holds more, which route drains faster) and report it honestly.

tracks.name: Reading and writing the working word

themes.description: Rated tags, warning labels, ingredient lists — the short texts the working world obeys, and how to read one completely.
themes.transfer_check: Read one real safety or rating label aloud, then state what it permits, what it forbids, and what it never says.

themes.description: Writing steps the way the trades need them — one action per line, in order, testable — because ambiguity on a jobsite costs.
themes.transfer_check: Write instructions for a small real task and have somebody follow them exactly, without you speaking, to a working result.

themes.description: Plans, symbols and the legend — reading a simple drawing the way a builder does, from title block to scale.
themes.transfer_check: Draw a labeled plan of a real room to a stated scale that lets somebody find one hidden object from it.

themes.description: Finding the one page that matters in a thick book — the tradesperson's fast reading: index, headings, diagrams first.
themes.transfer_check: Given a real manual (appliance, tool or car), find the answer to a stated question and cite the page you found it on.

themes.description: The steward's log, the watch log, the shift note — writing what happened so the next crew starts smart.
themes.transfer_check: Keep a log of one real activity, then hand it to somebody who continues the task using only what you wrote.

themes.description: Every craft's vocabulary is exact — joist and stud, live and neutral, port and starboard — and precision of word is precision of work.
themes.transfer_check: Teach somebody five exact terms from one trade, then have them use each correctly describing a real object.

themes.theme: The estimate is persuasion with numbers
themes.description: The written bid as an argument — clear scope, honest price, plain terms — and why the clearest writer often wins the job.
themes.transfer_check: Write a five-sentence bid for a small task that states scope, price and one term, and have a reader say what they'd ask before signing.

themes.description: Asking a working person real questions — open, specific, respectful — and listening for the detail worth writing down.
themes.transfer_check: Prepare five questions, interview somebody about their work, and write the one paragraph that captures what surprised you.

themes.description: Narrating work honestly — beginning, struggle, fix, finish — the crew's story told so the next crew learns from it.
themes.transfer_check: Write or tell the true story of one thing you built or fixed, including the mistake, to an audience that asks questions.

themes.description: Permits in windows, meeting agendas, the posted schedule — the civic texts of the working city, and how to read what they commit.
themes.transfer_check: Find one real posted permit, notice or agenda in your area and explain to somebody what it authorizes and who granted it.

themes.description: Streets, mains, wires, levees — a city as the sum of finished jobs, most of them invisible until they fail.
themes.transfer_check: Walk one block and list ten pieces of built work in order of what would be missed first if it stopped.

themes.description: Bonds, budgets, councils and boards — the civic machinery that turns taxes into pump stations and schools.
themes.transfer_check: Find one real public project in your parish or city budget and name the body that approved it and the money that funds it.

themes.theme: A short history of the union
themes.description: Why workers organized — hours, safety, the wage — and what apprenticeship halls did for the people who built your city.
themes.transfer_check: Tell the story of one real historical labor milestone, from a source you can name, to somebody who hadn't heard it.

themes.description: New Orleans on its river, Oakland on its bay, San Francisco on its gate — how working water shaped where people live.
themes.transfer_check: For one of the network's regions, explain from a map why the city stands where it does and what still moves through it.

themes.theme: The strike, the deal and the contract
themes.description: How disagreement at work becomes negotiation — the contract as a civic document both sides sign and both sides keep.
themes.transfer_check: Role-play a two-side negotiation over a classroom rule to a written one-line agreement both sides initial.

themes.description: Codes, permits and inspections as public promises — why the stamp on the drawing protects people who never read it.
themes.transfer_check: Explain, using one real example (an elevator plate, a restaurant grade, a permit), who inspected it and who is protected.

themes.description: Who restores the grid, drains the street, reopens the school — the working city's emergency shape, from Gulf hurricanes to Bay quakes.
themes.transfer_check: Chart which crews, in what order, brought one real past storm's neighborhood back — from news or a firsthand account.

themes.description: Who historically got the good trades and who was kept out — and what halls, schools and laws have done to open the door.
themes.transfer_check: Compare an old and a new photograph or roster of the same trade and describe, with respect, what changed and what still should.

themes.description: Apprenticeship as a public institution — registered programs, journey cards, and the taxes and codes that stand behind them.
themes.transfer_check: Chart the registered apprenticeship path for one trade in your region from the program's own public materials.

themes.theme: Your seat in the working city
themes.description: The learner as a future voter, neighbor and maybe tradesperson — where to stand on the next bond, the next hall, the next storm.
themes.transfer_check: Attend or watch one real public meeting that touches built work and report the one decision you would have voted on, and how.
